newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Howard government seen winning Telstra bill.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Howard government seen winning Telstra bill.

text.p: Australia's main non-government parties, the Labor opposition and the Democrats, both assume that the key Independent senators will let the government partially privatise telecoms carrier Telstra Corp.

"We will vote against it until the very end according to our principles and I do urge (Independent) senators (Mal) Colston and (Brian) Harradine to reconsider," Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot told reporters.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley reflected that the battle to prevent Telstra's privatisation was lost when the Liberal-National government won the March election.
"I think the simple fact of the matter is that Telstra was in all probability gone when the people voted against the Labor Party," he told reporters.

"I think that's an important thing for people to understand. "When the people voted last time even though they have not on every opinion poll wanted to see Telstra privatised, they voted for a government that would do it and therefore, it's done."
The Senate, the upper house of parliament, continued its debate on the Telstra privatisation bill on Thursday, the government revealing key concessions to the Independents.
The government needs Harradine and Colston because it is two votes short of a majority in the Senate and all other non-government senators are opposed to the sale.
Colston, who has said his votes would depend on government mandates, said during Thursday's debate he thought the government did have a mandate to sell Telstra.
In the past he has said his main concern about the Telstra sale was its impact on jobs outside of the main cities.
Communications Minister Richard Alston answered that, saying the government would direct A$250 million of the Telstra sale proceeds into a fund to develop rural telecoms infrastructure.
Colston himself had already said that he expected his concerns to be met.
Harradine, a Tasmanian, also had concerns about jobs that the same fund seems to address.
Alston also announced that the existing lure -- a fund for environmental repair -- had been sweetened by increasing its allocation to A$1.1 billion from A$1.0 billion.
It would particularly look after environmental concerns in Tasmania, he said.
Harradine himself revealed a deal with the government.
Harradine has always said he would like to see the government raise cash from Telstra by redeemable preference shares, rather than sale of equity.
The government has rejected that, but Harradine said he and the government had agreed to amend the legislation so that Telstra could not be sold before a committee examined his proposal.
The legislation would allow for either type of transaction -- sale or preference shares -- and the government could chose one of them after the committee reported.
Both Independents assisted the government with the necessary intermediate votes on the Telstra bill on Thursday.
A final vote on the bill, the Telstra (Dilution of Public Ownership) Bill, is expected on Monday.
The government expects the sale of a third of Telstra to raise about A$8 billion.
